name: harbour-lights-ep3
notes: Hand-authored fixture. ~40 min of interview, human web cut of 13 beats. Synthetic material cannot validate the product — only real pairs can. This exists to prove the harness and to check the metric discriminates.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Whenever you're ready. Just talk to me, not the camera.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Um. Right. Where do you want me to start?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My father kept his boat in the east basin for forty-three years. The Sigrun. She hasn't left the harbour since March, and she won't again.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Sorry, was that alright? I can do it again.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: People keep saying the harbour is closing. It isn't closing. It's being closed. There's a difference and everybody here knows exactly what it is.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: The dredging survey came back in, I want to say, February. Maybe March.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Nobody from the department has been down here. Not once. They've seen photographs.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Who made the decision?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: That depends who you ask, which is rather the point.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: There's a lot of paperwork. Forms about forms.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I've been harbour master for nineteen years. I have signed off on every vessel that's come through that gate. And in February I signed the notice that says they can't.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The tonnage thresholds moved in twenty-three and again in twenty-five, so a fleet that was compliant on Monday was non-compliant on Tuesday without anybody doing anything differently.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I don't blame the council. I blame the arithmetic. The council just read it out.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The gate mechanism is from nineteen sixty-eight. It still works. Everything here still works, that's the thing.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: We had an inspection in April. Passed it.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: And the boats that are left?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: There were sixty-two boats working out of here when I took over from my father. Sixty-two. There are nine.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Two are going to Thorshofn. Three are being sold south. The rest of us are waiting to see what the compensation looks like, and nobody will tell us.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: I mean the compensation, sorry, the transition package. That's what they call it.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: You can measure a harbour by the ice plant. If the ice plant runs, the harbour is alive. Ours stopped in April and nobody has asked me to start it again.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: There's a rota for the lights. I still do it.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My daughter asked me last week whether she should learn the boat. And I didn't have an answer for her. That's the first time that's happened.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: She's good with the engine. Better than I was at that age.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Do you think it could have gone differently?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Yes. That's the part I can't put down.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: If the survey had come back a year earlier there'd have been money in the coastal fund. A year. That's all it was.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The fund closed in twenty-four. Reallocated.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I've written to them four times. I get a reference number back.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: The east basin freezes first. Always has. My father used to say you could set your calendar by it.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: We used to have a festival in June. Stopped that in twenty-two, nothing to do with any of this.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: What happens to the buildings?

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Sold, probably. Somebody will want the view.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: There's a company been round twice. Photographs, tape measures. Nobody's told me anything.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: I'm not sentimental about it. I want to be clear about that. It's a job. It was a job.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: But you don't do a job for thirty years without it being something else as well.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: [overlapping] no but that's exactly what I. Sorry, go on.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Would I do it again? Yes. Obviously yes. That was never the question.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The question is what we tell the ones coming up. And I don't have that.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: [off mic] Do you want the bit about the ice again?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: It's a working harbour. That's not a description, it's a category. Once you lose the category you don't get it back.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I'll be the last one out. Somebody has to lock it.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Anything you want to add?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: No. I think that's it, really.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: There's a plaque somewhere about the eighteen-ninety-four storm. I should find that before they take it.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My father would have argued. He'd have gone to every meeting. I've been to two.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: That's not defeat, by the way. That's arithmetic as well.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: You get used to the sound. And then you notice it's gone.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Thank you. That was great.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Can you say your name and what you do, just for the record.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Margret Olsen. I fish, or I did.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Do you want me in this bit or shall I wait outside?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: The survey was commissioned by the port authority, not the council. People get that wrong.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: There are two basins. East and west. West silted up years ago.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Tide's low this morning. You can see the sill.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: It's not a big harbour. It was never a big harbour.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The lights are on a timer now. Used to be manual.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My grandfather was here too, but he was crew, not skipper.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Sorry, one second, there's a van going past.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Shall I wait? I'll wait.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The quota paperwork goes to Reykjavik and comes back six weeks later.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: We used to land haddock mostly. Some cod. Depends on the year.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: There's a chandlery on the corner. Closed Tuesdays.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: You'd get maybe two hundred days a year you could go out. Weather.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I keep the logbooks. All of them, back to when I started.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: It's not that people don't care. It's that caring isn't a submission.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Tell me about the ice plant.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: The co-op ran it. Six of us on the committee.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Electricity bill on that thing was extraordinary.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Um, what was the question? Sorry.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: You have to sound the horn before the gate moves. Regulation.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My husband worked at the plant. Different plant, up the road.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Can we go back to the survey for a moment?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: It's forty pages and about six of them matter.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I read all forty. Twice.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: There's a consultation window. It closed in June.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I did submit. I have the reference number here somewhere.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: People assume it's romantic. It's cold and it's wet and the money is bad.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The moorings are numbered but the numbers don't run in order. Never have.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: I sold the small boat in twenty-three. Kept the Sigrun.

beats.speaker: Interviewer
beats.text: Is there anyone else we should talk to?

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: Talk to Erla. She'll tell you about the co-op.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Erla's in Akureyri now, mind.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: The nets go to a yard in Denmark. They pay by weight.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: I've got a key to everything here. Every door.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: It's not a museum. That's what I'd say to them. It's not a museum yet.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: The tide gauge is the oldest instrument on the coast, apparently.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: You want the truth, I've stopped reading the letters.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Somebody suggested a heritage trail. I didn't say anything.

beats.speaker: Margret Olsen
beats.text: My father would have known who to ring. I don't.

beats.speaker: Jonas Berg
beats.text: Anyway. That's the harbour.
